name: Determinism
statement: Given the state of the world and the laws of nature, only one future is possible.
meaning: Causal determinism is the thesis that every event, or the total state of the world at any time, is the inevitable consequence of antecedent events together with the laws of nature. On a standard formulation, the world is governed by determinism if and only if, given a specified way things are at a time, the way things go thereafter is fixed as a matter of natural law, so that the past and the laws together leave exactly one possible future. The classic image of determinism is Laplace's demon, Pierre-Simon Laplace's picture of an intelligence that, knowing the precise position and momentum of every particle and all the forces acting, could compute the entire past and future of the universe with certainty. It is important to distinguish determinism from several things it is often confused with. It is a claim about the world and its laws, not about predictability, which is epistemic, since a deterministic world may be unpredictable in practice, as chaos theory shows through sensitive dependence on initial conditions. It differs from fatalism, the idea that certain events will happen no matter what we do, and from predestination, and it is not the same as mere causation. Determinism comes in kinds, including causal or nomological, logical, and theological. Whether our own world is deterministic is an open empirical question, since classical physics is largely deterministic but quantum mechanics appears, on standard interpretations, to introduce fundamental indeterminism.
mechanism: Determinism is a claim about how the states of the world are related across time by the laws of nature. If the world is deterministic, then a complete specification of its state at any one time, together with the laws, entails a unique complete state at every other time, past and future; nothing is left open. Laplace dramatized this by imagining an intellect that, given the exact mechanical state of everything and unlimited computational power, would find the future and the past equally present before its eyes, with nothing uncertain. The demon expresses determinism but also invites a confusion the concept must resist: determinism does not require that anyone, or any demon, can actually predict the future. Predictability is an epistemic matter about what can be known or computed, and a fully deterministic system can be practically unpredictable, as chaotic systems are, because tiny uncertainties in the initial conditions grow so fast that long-run prediction fails even though the evolution is fixed. Determinism must likewise be kept apart from fatalism, which holds that an outcome will occur regardless of the causal route, often by appeal to fate or divine will, whereas determinism says outcomes occur through the causal chain, so that what we do is part of what determines the result. The doctrine takes several forms: causal or nomological determinism concerns physical events and laws; logical determinism concerns the truth of statements about the future, as in Aristotle's sea-battle puzzle about future contingents; and theological determinism concerns divine foreknowledge and predestination. Whether the actual world is deterministic turns on physics, where quantum mechanics on the standard interpretation introduces genuine chance, though deterministic interpretations such as Bohmian mechanics exist.

examples.text: An intelligence knowing every particle's state and all forces could, Laplace imagined, compute the whole past and future with certainty.
A deterministic world can be unpredictable in practice, as chaotic systems show through sensitive dependence on initial conditions.
Standard quantum mechanics appears to introduce fundamental chance, so whether our world is deterministic is an open question.

variants.name: Kinds of determinism
variants.text: Causal or nomological, logical, and theological determinism, concerning physical events, future statements, and divine foreknowledge.

variants.name: Determinism versus fatalism
variants.text: Determinism holds outcomes occur through the causal chain, while fatalism holds they occur no matter what one does.

whyItMatters: Determinism is a pivotal thesis in metaphysics and the philosophy of science, and above all it is the fulcrum of the free will debate. Whether human beings have the kind of freedom required for moral responsibility is standardly framed as the question of whether free will is compatible with determinism, so the compatibilism-incompatibilism divide, and with it our understanding of praise, blame, and desert, turns on what determinism is and whether it holds. Beyond free will, determinism raises deep questions about the structure of nature, the status of the laws, and the relation between the physical and the mental. Its careful formulation forces crucial distinctions that guard against confusion: between the metaphysical claim that the future is fixed and the epistemic matter of whether it can be predicted, between determinism and fatalism, and between deterministic laws and mere causal influence. The image of Laplace's demon has become a touchstone for thinking about physical law, chance, and knowledge, and the arrival of quantum mechanics turned the truth of determinism into a live scientific question rather than a philosophical assumption.

working.text: specify the complete state of the world at a time together with the laws of nature.
hold that these together entail exactly one possible way things go thereafter.
keep determinism apart from predictability, from fatalism, and from mere causation.

limits: Determinism must be handled with care, and several of its features are easy to misstate or are genuinely open. Whether the actual world is deterministic is not settled by philosophy but by physics, and here the situation is unresolved: classical Newtonian mechanics is largely deterministic, but standard quantum mechanics on the Copenhagen interpretation introduces apparently irreducible chance, in the timing of radioactive decay and the probabilities of the Born rule, while deterministic interpretations such as Bohmian mechanics and many-worlds remain live options, so the empirical question is undecided. The relation of determinism to free will is itself contested, since compatibilists and incompatibilists disagree about whether a fixed future threatens responsibility. Some notions in the vicinity, such as adequate determinism, the idea that macroscopic events are effectively determined even if micro-events are not, are less standard and best attributed to their proponents rather than to the core literature. And the precise dating of Laplace's statement, the 1814 French essay and its various editions and translations, and the exact wording of his image, reward care.
misreadings: Determinism is not the same as predictability; a deterministic world can be unpredictable in practice, as chaos shows, and predictability is about what can be known, not about what is fixed. It is not fatalism, which holds outcomes will occur regardless of causes, whereas determinism makes what we do part of the causal chain that produces outcomes. And it is not simply the claim that events have causes, but the stronger claim that the state and laws together fix a unique future, so treating determinism as predictability, as fatalism, or as mere causation, misreads the thesis.
origin: The thesis, classically expressed by Laplace's demon, that the complete state of the world at a time together with the laws of nature fixes a unique past and future, central to the free will debate and to the philosophy of science.

sources.text: Causal Determinism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the standard formulation of determinism as the state at a time fixing the way things go thereafter as a matter of natural law, Laplace's demon, the distinction from predictability, fatalism, and mere causation, and the bearing of classical and quantum physics on whether the world is deterministic.

Foreknowledge and Free Will, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — theological and logical determinism, divine foreknowledge and predestination, and the relation of determinism to freedom, with the Aristotelian problem of future contingents.
